summary: This standards-track document defines the ORIGIN frame for HTTP/2. A server sends it to tell a client which origins it is able to serve over a given connection. That helps clients decide when they can reuse a connection for other hostnames instead of opening new ones.

eli5.summary: A shop worker says, 'You can ask me about these items too.' The ORIGIN frame is a server telling you which websites it can answer for, so you do not need a new line.

subtitle: How an HTTP/2 server tells a client exactly which websites a single connection can be used for.

tldr.problem: HTTP/2 lets a client reuse one connection for several origins, but when the connection cannot serve one of them the client only finds out from a 421 (Misdirected Request) error, which costs latency. Proving authority with both DNS and the certificate is also described as onerous.
tldr.mechanism: A new HTTP/2 frame type, ORIGIN (0xc), lets the server list the origins it considers part of the connection's Origin Set. Clients that understand it use the set when deciding what the connection is authoritative for, and may skip some DNS lookups.
tldr.outcome: Clients can reuse connections more confidently and avoid some round trips. Skipping DNS creates new risks, so the RFC tells clients to find other ways to trust the certificate.

facts.label: Flags
facts.value: None defined; 0x1, 0x2, 0x4, 0x8 reserved for incompatible changes

today: RFC 8336 is a Proposed Standard, and the unit metadata shows it has not been obsoleted or updated. It builds on RFC 7540.

sections.title: Why a Server Needs to Name Its Origins
sections.content:
HTTP/2 (RFC 7540) lets a client coalesce different origins onto the same connection when certain conditions are met. Sometimes the connection turns out not to be usable for a coalesced origin, so the 421 (Misdirected Request) status code was defined. A client can recover from a 421, but at the cost of added latency.

This document defines a new frame type, ORIGIN, so that servers can say up front for which origins a connection is usable. It also relaxes HTTP/2's requirement to establish server authority using both DNS and the certificate, which the authors call onerous. Dropping some DNS lookups also removes the latency of those lookups.
sections.eli5: Imagine knocking on the wrong door and being sent away, then trying another. It is faster if the person at the door says up front which questions they can answer.

sections.title: The ORIGIN Frame Format
sections.content:
The ORIGIN frame type is 0xc (decimal 12). Its payload holds zero or more Origin-Entry fields. Each entry is length-delimited: a 16-bit unsigned Origin-Len gives the length in octets, followed by an optional ASCII-Origin string, which is the ASCII serialization of an origin (RFC 6454) that the sender asserts the connection is or could be authoritative for.

The frame defines no flags, though future updates may define some.
sections.eli5: The frame is a list of website names. Each name comes with a note saying how long it is, so the reader knows where one ends and the next begins.

sections.title: Processing ORIGIN Frames
sections.content:
ORIGIN is a non-critical extension, so endpoints that do not support it can safely ignore it. A receiving client uses it to build the Origin Set.

  • It MUST be sent on stream 0; on any other stream it is invalid and MUST be ignored.
  • It is only valid on connections using the h2 identifier (or where a protocol definition nominates it) and MUST be ignored on h2c.
  • The first four flags (0x1, 0x2, 0x4, 0x8) are reserved for backwards-incompatible changes, so a frame with any of them set is ignored unless the client understands the flag.
  • It is processed hop by hop: an intermediary MUST NOT forward it, and a client using a proxy MUST ignore ORIGIN frames from it.
  • An entry that fails to parse as an ASCII-serialized origin MUST be ignored.

Wildcard names such as *.example.com are not supported in entries. So a server using a wildcard certificate that sends ORIGIN effectively disables any origins it does not list, for clients that understand the frame.
sections.eli5: The rules say where the list may come from and when to ignore it, like only trusting a note that came straight from the shop worker and not one passed along by someone in between.

sections.title: The Origin Set
sections.content:
The Origin Set is the set of origins a connection might be used for. By default it is uninitialized, and clients then apply the ordinary coalescing rules from Section 9.1.1 of RFC 7540.

When the first ORIGIN frame is successfully processed, the set is created containing an initial origin: scheme https, the host from the Server Name Indication value in lower case (or the server's IP address if there is no SNI), and the server's port. The frame's entries then add origins to the set, incrementally across frames.

A 421 response also changes the set: the client removes the origin of the corresponding request from it, if present.

With an alternative service on a different port, the initial origin uses the port actually in use. For an alternative service at x.example.net port 8443, the initial origin is https://example.com:8443, so https://example.com must be listed explicitly in the ORIGIN frame to be used.
sections.eli5: The Origin Set is the list of shops one phone line can reach. It starts with just the shop you dialed, and the shop worker can add more names to it.

sections.title: Authority, Push, and Coalescing
sections.content:
Once a connection has an Origin Set, clients that implement this specification MUST NOT treat the connection as authoritative for an origin outside the set. They SHOULD use it for all requests to origins in the set that it is authoritative for, unless there are operational reasons to open a new connection.

The set does not replace certificate checks. The server must still present a certificate that passes the checks in Section 9.1.1 of RFC 7540, including that the host matches a dNSName in the subjectAltName field. What changes is that clients MAY avoid consulting DNS for new requests to origins in the set, which brings the risks described under security.

Because ORIGIN can change the set over time, a client may hold more than one viable connection to an origin. Clients SHOULD NOT send new requests on a connection whose Origin Set is a proper subset of another's, and SHOULD close it once outstanding requests finish. Advertising an alternative service does not change the Origin Set or whether a server is authoritative.
sections.eli5: The list says which shops the line may reach, but the shop still has to show its ID. If two lines reach the same shops, you use the bigger one and hang up the smaller one.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Clients that blindly trust the ORIGIN frame's contents are vulnerable to many attacks. The main risk comes from skipping DNS: an attacker who holds a valid certificate no longer needs to be on the path to redirect traffic. Instead of altering DNS, they only need to convince the user to visit another website so connections to the target coalesce onto the attacker's connection.

Clients that skip DNS should therefore find another way to be confident the certificate is legitimate. The RFC suggests requiring proof of inclusion in a Certificate Transparency log (RFC 6962), or a recent OCSP response (RFC 6960) showing the certificate was not revoked.

The size of the Origin Set is unbounded by this specification, so an attacker could use it to exhaust client resources. Clients can watch their state commitment and close the connection if it grows too high.
sections.eli5: If you stop double-checking who someone really is, a trickster with a fake badge could slip in. So you need some other way to check the badge, and you should not let anyone hand you an endless list.

sections.title: Operational Advice for Servers
sections.content:
Servers are not obliged to send ORIGIN or to list every origin they could serve. An empty ORIGIN frame tells the client to use the connection only for the SNI-based origin. A payload lists more.

The frame is most useful when sent early, ideally before any HEADERS or PUSH_PROMISE frames, so the client knows before it sees links that might start a new connection. If very many origins would add visible latency, a server might send a core set first and expand it later, for example when the connection is idle. Even so, senders are encouraged to include as many origins as practical in one frame, since a set split across many frames can lead to suboptimal client decisions. Origins must be case-normalized before serialization, and servers hosting alternative services must list those origins explicitly.
sections.eli5: It is best to read out the list of shops before the customer starts wandering off. A short list first and more later is fine, but one complete list is easiest to use.
